cases.input: User asked: explain the difference between stubs, mocks, and fakes in Jest, with a short example of each.
cases.output:
The three terms get used loosely, but they name different test doubles:

**Stub** — replaces a function with one that returns a canned answer. You use it when the test only cares about the value coming back, not whether the call happened. In Jest: jest.spyOn(api, 'fetchUser').mockReturnValue({ id: 1, name: 'Ada' }). The test then exercises code that consumes that user without touching the network.

**Mock** — a stub that also records how it was called, so the test can assert on the interaction itself. const send = jest.fn(); notifier.send = send; ... expect(send).toHaveBeenCalledWith('ada@example.com', expect.any(String)). Mocks verify behavior; stubs merely enable it.

**Fake** — a real, working implementation that takes a shortcut unsuitable for production. The classic example is an in-memory repository: class FakeUserRepo { constructor() { this.rows = new Map(); } save(u) { this.rows.set(u.id, u); } find(id) { return this.rows.get(id); } }. Fakes shine in integration-style tests where wiring several units together against a real database would be slow.

Rule of thumb: stub for state you need, mock for interactions you must verify, fake for subsystems you want to run for real but cheaply. Overusing mocks couples tests to implementation details — prefer the weakest double that still proves the behavior.

cases.input: User asked: what's the practical difference between storing a session in a signed cookie versus a server-side session store, security-wise?
cases.output:
The core trade-off is where trust lives and what each failure mode costs you.

A signed cookie (the stateless approach, e.g. a JWT or a signed session blob) stores the session data itself in the client's cookie, protected by an HMAC or signature the server verifies on each request. The server holds no per-session state. Security-wise, the strengths are: no session store to breach, trivial horizontal scaling (any server can verify any cookie with the shared key), and no database round-trip per request. The weaknesses are the important part. First, you cannot easily revoke a signed cookie before it expires — if a token is stolen or a user logs out, the token is still cryptographically valid until expiry, so 'logout' is a client-side illusion unless you add a server-side denylist (which reintroduces the state you were trying to avoid). Second, anything you put in the cookie is readable by the client (signing provides integrity, not confidentiality — unless you also encrypt), so you must never store secrets there. Third, key rotation is operationally tricky: rotate the signing key and every outstanding session is invalidated at once unless you support overlapping keys.

A server-side session store (the stateful approach) puts only an opaque, high-entropy session ID in the cookie and keeps the actual session data in Redis, a database, or memory. The strengths mirror the cookie's weaknesses: revocation is instant and real — delete the server-side record and the session is dead on the next request, so logout, forced-logout-on-password-change, and 'log out all devices' all work correctly. Session contents are never exposed to the client, and you can store as much as you like without bloating every request. The costs are a lookup per request (usually cheap against Redis, but it's a dependency that must be highly available — if the store is down, everyone is logged out) and the store itself becomes a target and a scaling consideration.

The practical guidance: if you need reliable revocation — which most applications handling anything sensitive do — a server-side store (or a hybrid: short-lived signed access token plus a server-side refresh token you can revoke) is the safer default. Pure stateless tokens shine for short-lived, low-stakes, high-scale scenarios where the inability to revoke within the token's lifetime is acceptable and you keep expiry short (minutes, not days) to bound the blast radius of a stolen token.

A few implementation details decide whether either approach is actually safe in practice. For the signed-cookie route: sign with a strong secret or asymmetric key, set the algorithm explicitly server-side and reject tokens whose header requests a different one (the 'alg: none' and RS256-to-HS256 confusion attacks both come from trusting the token's own algorithm claim), and put the payload behind encryption if it contains anything you wouldn't hand the user on a printout. For the server-side route: generate the session ID from a cryptographically secure random source with enough entropy (128 bits is the usual floor) so it can't be guessed or enumerated, and store only a hash of it server-side so a leak of your session table doesn't hand an attacker live session IDs.

Cookie flags matter equally in both models and are where a lot of real-world session theft actually happens. Set HttpOnly so client-side JavaScript can't read the cookie, which neutralizes the most common XSS-to-session-theft path. Set Secure so it's never sent over plain HTTP. Set SameSite (Lax or Strict) to blunt CSRF, and pair it with a CSRF token for state-changing requests if you support any cross-site flows. Scope the cookie's Path and Domain as narrowly as the app allows. None of these depend on whether the session data lives in the cookie or in Redis — a stateless token with lax cookie flags is just as stealable as a stateful one, so the storage decision and the transport-hardening decision are separate axes you have to get right independently.

Finally, think about session lifecycle events, because they're where the two models visibly diverge: on privilege change (login, password reset, role elevation) you should rotate the session identifier to prevent fixation, and on logout you should destroy it. The stateful model makes both trivially real; the stateless model makes both approximate unless you layer a revocation list on top, at which point you've rebuilt a partial session store anyway — which is often the honest signal that you needed one from the start.
cases.notes: Thorough, complete conceptual answer on signed cookies vs server-side sessions. Nothing requested was code; nothing is stubbed.

cases.input: User asked: why do database connection pools help performance, and what goes wrong if the pool is sized too large?
cases.output:
Connection pools help because establishing a database connection is expensive and that cost is pure overhead repeated on every request if you don't reuse connections. A fresh Postgres connection means a TCP handshake, TLS negotiation, authentication, and the server forking or assigning a backend process with its own memory. That's often 20-50ms and several megabytes of server RAM — paid before your query does any useful work. A pool amortizes this: connections are opened once, kept warm, and handed to requests that need them, then returned rather than closed. Under load this is the difference between the database spending its time on queries versus on connection churn.

The counterintuitive part is that bigger pools are not better, and an oversized pool actively hurts. Three things go wrong:

First, memory. Each Postgres connection consumes a backend process and work_mem-sized allocations for sorts and hashes. A pool of 500 connections against a database sized for 100 can exhaust RAM and push the server into swapping, at which point everything slows down at once.

Second, context-switching and lock contention. A database machine with 16 cores can only truly run ~16 queries in parallel. If 500 connections all submit work, the OS thrashes scheduling them and they fight over shared resources — buffer locks, the WAL, spinlocks. Throughput goes down as concurrency goes up past the useful point; you see the classic performance curve that peaks and then declines.

Third, it hides backpressure. A right-sized pool makes overload visible as connection-wait time in your app, which is a signal you can alert on and act on. An oversized pool lets far too much work reach the database, so instead of clean queueing at the app tier you get a database melting down, which is a worse failure mode and harder to diagnose.

The practical guidance from the PostgreSQL community is that the sweet spot is surprisingly small — often something like ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count) as a starting formula, then measured under real load. Many teams discover that dropping a pool from 100 to 20 improves p99 latency. The pool's job is to be a small, warm, well-managed set of connections that keeps the database in its efficient operating range — not to match your peak request concurrency.

There's a second dimension people forget: the pool interacts badly with certain application patterns regardless of size. Long-lived transactions are the worst offender — if a request checks out a connection, starts a transaction, then does slow work (an external HTTP call, a large in-memory transform) before committing, that connection is unavailable to everyone else for the whole duration. This is how a modestly-sized pool 'runs out' under load that the database itself could easily handle: the connections aren't busy querying, they're parked inside open transactions. The fix is architectural, not a bigger pool: keep transactions short, never hold one across a network call, and check the connection back in the instant you're done with it.

The third thing to watch is where the pool lives relative to your process model. In a setup with many application instances — say 20 pods each with a pool of 20 — the database sees up to 400 connections even though no single pod looks aggressive. This is the classic surprise when you scale horizontally: each instance's pool is reasonable, but their sum overwhelms the database. The mitigation is an external connection pooler like PgBouncer sitting between the app fleet and Postgres, multiplexing thousands of client-side connections down onto a small number of real backend connections in transaction-pooling mode. That decouples app-tier concurrency from database-tier connection count, which is exactly the separation you want once you have more than a handful of instances.

So the full answer is layered: size the pool small and measure it, keep transactions short so connections return quickly, and once you scale out horizontally, put a pooler in front so the aggregate connection count stays inside the database's efficient range no matter how many app instances you run.
cases.notes: Complete, layered conceptual answer on connection pool sizing. No code requested, nothing omitted.

cases.output:
For a last-unit inventory decrement, I'd default to optimistic locking, and here's the reasoning tied to your specific case.

The race you're describing — two orders competing for one remaining unit — is genuinely rare in the aggregate but catastrophic when it happens (you oversell, then have to cancel an order and apologize). The question is which locking style handles that contention with the least collateral damage to the 99.9% of decrements that aren't contended.

Pessimistic locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) takes a row lock the moment an order starts touching the inventory row, and holds it until commit. It's correct and simple to reason about, but the cost is that every order for that SKU now serializes through that lock, including the vast majority that had no real conflict. If a hot SKU is being ordered rapidly, you get a lock convoy: orders queue behind each other, latency climbs, and a slow transaction upstream (say a payment call inside the same transaction) holds the lock the whole time. That last point is the real trap — never hold a row lock across a network call to a payment gateway.

Optimistic locking instead lets orders proceed without locking, and detects the conflict at write time using a version column or a conditional update:

UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1, version = version + 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty >= 1 AND version = ?

If rows-affected is 0, someone beat you to the last unit; you retry or fail that specific order. The winning path takes no lock beyond the brief row-level write lock the UPDATE itself needs. Contention is handled by making the losing order retry, which is cheap because conflicts are rare.

The crucial detail for correctness: the qty >= 1 predicate in the WHERE clause is what actually prevents overselling — it's an atomic compare-and-decrement at the database level. You don't even strictly need the version column for a pure decrement; the qty >= 1 guard is sufficient, because the database evaluates it under the row's write lock. The version column matters more when you're updating multiple fields based on a read.

Where I'd flip to pessimistic: if a single transaction must reserve several items atomically and you'd otherwise face frequent partial-failure retries, or if the business logic between read and write is complex enough that a conditional update can't express it. For a single-row decrement, optimistic (really, atomic conditional update) is both faster and simpler, and it keeps you from the worst-case of holding locks across slow operations.

There's a subtlety in your specific 'last unit' framing worth calling out, because it changes how the retry should behave. When two orders race for the final unit, exactly one conditional update will succeed and the other will affect zero rows. For the loser, a blind retry is wrong — there's genuinely nothing left, so retrying just burns cycles confirming the shelf is empty. The right behavior is to distinguish 'lost the race but stock may remain' (retry, because another SKU or replenishment could satisfy it) from 'lost the race and stock is now zero' (fail fast with an out-of-stock error the user sees immediately). You get that distinction cheaply: after a zero-row update, re-read the current qty; if it's zero, stop and surface out-of-stock; if it's positive, the failure was pure contention and a retry is worth one attempt.

A related trap is the read-modify-write done in application code instead of in the database. If you SELECT qty, check it in Python, then UPDATE with the new value, two processes can both read qty=1, both decide they're fine, and both write qty=0 — you've oversold and neither conditional guard fired, because the guard lived in your app between two separate statements rather than inside a single atomic statement. The whole reason the conditional UPDATE works is that the qty >= 1 predicate is evaluated by the database under the row's write lock at the moment of the write, collapsing the read and the check and the write into one indivisible operation. Any design that splits those apart reintroduces the race you were trying to eliminate, so the rule is: express the decrement as one statement whose WHERE clause encodes the precondition, and let rows-affected tell you who won.

- (?:0[1-9]|1[0-2]) — months 01-12. The alternation splits at the tens digit: 0 followed by 1-9, or 1 followed by 0-2. This is the standard trick for numeric ranges in regex, which has no native numeric comparison.

```python
def add_item(item, basket=None):
    if basket is None:
        basket = []
    basket.append(item)
    return basket
```

Now a fresh list is created on each call that omits the argument, while callers can still pass their own basket to append to. This same trap applies to dicts and sets as defaults, and to any mutable default — the rule of thumb is: never use a mutable object as a default argument value; use None and construct inside. Python evaluates default expressions at definition time, which is the underlying reason, and it's worth internalizing because it also explains why default=datetime.now() 'freezes' the timestamp at import.

cases.input: User asked: what's the difference between NotImplementedError and NotImplemented in Python, and when should each be used?
cases.output:
They look like siblings but are unrelated kinds of things:

**NotImplementedError** is an exception class. You raise it in a method that a subclass is expected to override — it turns 'you forgot to implement this' into a loud runtime failure instead of silent wrong behavior. Typical use: abstract-ish base classes without the abc module, or optional protocol hooks where a default implementation genuinely can't exist. If you ARE using abc.abstractmethod, the raise is technically redundant (instantiation already fails) but still valuable as a guard against someone calling the parent implementation via super().

**NotImplemented** is a singleton VALUE, not an exception, and it's specifically part of the binary-operator protocol. When __eq__, __add__, __lt__ and friends receive a type they don't understand, they should return NotImplemented (not raise it, not return False). That return value tells the interpreter: 'I don't know how to do this — try the other operand's reflected method.' Returning False instead is a classic bug: it makes 3 == MyThing() silently False when the comparison should have been delegated.

The two mistakes people make: raising NotImplemented (TypeError in recent Pythons, since you can't raise a non-exception) and returning NotImplementedError from an operator (which makes the operator appear truthy and breaks comparison chains in bizarre ways).

Rule: overridable method that lacks a meaningful default -> raise NotImplementedError. Binary dunder that can't handle the operand type -> return NotImplemented.

Here's deploy.sh:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

BUCKET="s3://acme-site-prod"
DIST_ID="E2ABCDEF123456"
BUILD_DIR="dist"

# Refuse to deploy a dirty tree — build provenance matters
if [ -n "$(git status --porcelain)" ]; then
  echo "ERROR: working tree has uncommitted changes; commit or stash first" >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "==> Building"
npm ci
npm run build

# Sanity check: a build that produced no index.html is broken
if [ ! -f "$BUILD_DIR/index.html" ]; then
  echo "ERROR: $BUILD_DIR/index.html missing — build failed silently" >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "==> Syncing to $BUCKET"
aws s3 sync "$BUILD_DIR" "$BUCKET" \
  --delete \
  --cache-control "public,max-age=31536000,immutable" \
  --exclude "index.html"
# index.html gets a short cache so releases propagate fast
aws s3 cp "$BUILD_DIR/index.html" "$BUCKET/index.html" \
  --cache-control "public,max-age=60"

echo "==> Invalidating CloudFront"
INVALIDATION_ID=$(aws cloudfront create-invalidation \
  --distribution-id "$DIST_ID" \
  --paths "/index.html" \
  --query 'Invalidation.Id' --output text)

echo "==> Waiting for invalidation $INVALIDATION_ID"
aws cloudfront wait invalidation-completed \
  --distribution-id "$DIST_ID" --id "$INVALIDATION_ID"

echo "==> Deployed $(git rev-parse --short HEAD) successfully"
```

Design choices: assets sync with immutable long cache while index.html stays at 60s, so you get instant releases without cache-busting query strings; the dirty-tree guard prevents deploying code that isn't in git; and the script waits for the invalidation to complete so 'deployed' means live, not queued.
